Key Research Thinking Patterns: Tract-Specific Microstructural Quantification: Leveraging automated deep learning segmentation and Magnetization Transfer Ratio (MTR) extraction to resolve inhomogeneous compressive damage in spinal cord white matter, correlating specific tract integrity (e.g., ventral reticulospinal tract) with clinical motor disability scores (mJOA) rather than relying on regional averages.

Interface Engineering for Photovoltaic Stability: Utilizing non-fullerene acceptors (e.g., Y7-BO) to passivate surface defects and modify the perovskite/electron transport layer interface, validated through DFT calculations and spectroscopic analyses (XPS, TOF-SIMS) to enhance power conversion efficiency and operational stability in large-area modules.

Multimodal Neurocognitive Correlation: Integrating resting-state fMRI functional connectivity analysis with standardized neuropsychological testing (RBANS, MoCA) to identify network-level biomarkers (e.g., Default Mode Network integrity) that predict cognitive performance subgroups in non-hospitalized post-COVID patients.

High-Resolution Temporal Network Dynamics: Applying k-means clustering to cortical source tomography of resting-state EEG to identify transient cortical co-activation patterns (<100 ms), demonstrating their spatial correspondence with time-averaged fMRI networks to reveal the fast temporal dynamics underlying classical brain connectivity.
Summary Description: Lei Ding is a principal investigator at the University of Oklahoma specializing in the intersection of biomedical engineering, neurosurgery, and materials science. His research focuses on two primary translational goals: advancing neuroimaging for spinal cord pathology and developing high-performance perovskite photovoltaics. In neuroscience, he employs deep learning-based segmentation and tract-specific MTR analysis to quantify white matter injury in Degenerative Cervical Myelopathy, while utilizing resting-state fMRI and EEG to characterize brain network dynamics in post-COVID cognitive impairment. In materials science, he engineers perovskite/electron transport layer interfaces using non-fullerene acceptors to enhance the efficiency and stability of large-area solar modules. His work bridges clinical neurology and industrial energy applications through rigorous quantitative imaging and interface modification strategies.
